steps.prompt: Reflect a shape in one mirror, then in a second mirror parallel to the first. The shape ends up where? Try it with a letter on squared paper.

cards.title: The moves
cards.body: Reflect over the $x$-axis: $(x, -y)$; over the $y$-axis: $(-x, y)$; over $y = x$: $(y, x)$. Rotate $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin: $(-y, x)$; $180^\circ$: $(-x, -y)$. Translations add to both coordinates. None of these change lengths or areas.

cards.title: Worked example: two moves
cards.problem: Reflect $(3, 5)$ over $y = x$, then rotate the image $180^\circ$ about the origin.

try.prompt: What is the $x$-coordinate after the reflection?

cards.title: Combining moves and symmetry
cards.body: Two reflections in parallel lines make a translation by twice the gap. Two reflections in lines that cross make a rotation by twice the angle between them. A regular $n$-gon has $n$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $n$.

try.prompt: What is the $x$-coordinate after the first mirror?

steps.text: Over $x = 7$: $(8, 1)$. The point moved $6$, twice the gap of $3$.

cards.title: The common trap: which way it turns
cards.body: $90^\circ$ counterclockwise is $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$; clockwise is $(y, -x)$. To turn about a point other than the origin, move that point to the origin first, turn, then move back.

prompts: How do you check that you turned a point the right way?
